source_document.body:
What changes when robots join the warehouse team? Manish Kapoor , Founder and CEO of Growth Catalyst Group , shares lessons from Archway’s Minnesota fulfillment center, including how employees’ jobs have changed and how to decide which tasks are worth automating .
What’s Related
Supply Chain 24/7: What led Archway to add robots at its Maple Grove fulfillment center?
Manish Kapoor: We didn’t start by saying, ‘we need robots.’ We started with the problem we were trying to solve. This was a joint initiative with Blackhawk Network, a fulfillment client of ours, that specializes in global branded payments with gift cards, eGifts, rewards and other payment products. Together, we looked at what the Maple Grove operation needed to deliver as demand grows. We focused on productivity, accuracy, speed, space and scalability.
Customers expect orders quickly, they expect them to be right, and they need flexibility as demand changes. We needed an operation that could respond to changing demand while making better use of our people and the space we already have.
RELATED STORIES: Six Trends Changing How Mobile Robots Work in Warehouses | Robots for the Rest of Us: Warehouse Automation Gets Easier
That led us to Quicktron’s goods-to-person solution. It combines high-density storage with tote-handling robots, tote transport robots and intelligent picking workstations. Instead of employees spending time walking through the warehouse to find inventory, the robots retrieve the right totes from storage and move them to the picking stations where our people fulfill the orders . It allows us to store more products in a relatively small footprint while moving thousands of product units through the system every hour. For me, that’s the important point. We didn’t choose automation because we wanted robots in the building. We defined what the operation needed to achieve, then found the technology that could help us achieve it.
SC247: Can you walk us through how the robots and employees work together to fill a gift card order?
“Customers expect orders quickly, they expect them to be right, and they need flexibility as demand changes”
Kapoor: It’s a goods-to-person system, so rather than having an employee walk through the warehouse to find and move inventory, the system brings the inventory to them.
Within the automation area, we have tote-handling robots working in a high-density storage system, tote transport robots and picking workstations. The robots retrieve and move the appropriate totes through the system and bring them to the workstation where our people can complete the picking process.
That takes a lot of unnecessary movement out of the job. Our employees can focus on fulfilling the order while the robots handle much of the movement of inventory around them.
That’s the relationship we want between people and automation. Use the technology for the work it is good at, and give our people better tools to do their jobs and the time back to focus on human-centric tasks
SC247: You report a 300% increase in productivity. What did you measure, and what was the comparison?
Kapoor: The improvement is more than 300% in productivity within the automation area, compared with the previous process. Before implementing the technology, we established a baseline so we could understand whether it was solving the problems we had identified. Productivity was obviously a major measure, but we were also looking at accuracy, speed and how effectively we could use the available space. The system can now process thousands of product units every hour, and we’ve reduced time to market by 50%. That means we can get products where they need to go much faster while making the fulfillment operation more responsive. That’s the important part of measuring automation.
SC247: How have employees’ day-to-day jobs changed since the robots arrived?
Kapoor: The biggest change is that the product comes to the person, rather than the person spending so much time going to the product. In a traditional warehouse process, there can be a lot of walking and movement involved in finding inventory and getting it where it needs to go. The goods-to-person system takes a lot of that movement out of the process.
Our people remain a critical part of the operation. What we’re doing is giving them technology that helps them work more efficiently and allows us to process more volume with the workforce we have. That’s how I think about automation. It’s not robots versus people. It’s about how you bring the two together to build a better process.
SC247: What was the hardest part of getting the robots up and running?
Kapoor: With any automation project, the robot is only one part of the picture. The operating process, software , data and people must work together.
We had an advantage because we have our own warehouse management platform, so we had full control of the software side which helped make the software integration smooth. But, you still need to think through how technology fits into the whole operation, how your people are going to work with it and how you measure whether it is doing what you expected.
I often say transformation takes a village. Archway, Blackhawk Network and Quicktron all brought different expertise to this project. Getting those pieces working together is what turns a technology project into an operational improvement.
“With any automation project, the robot is only one part of the picture. The operating process, software, data and people must work together.”
SC247: Why did you choose these robots, and where do you see humanoid robots fitting into warehouse work?
Kapoor: We started with the problem, not the technology. We knew what we wanted to improve in the operation, and we established the criteria before selecting a solution. We looked at productivity, quality, speed, how effectively we could use the space, and whether the system could scale with the customer. Quicktron’s robotic solution fit those requirements.
The ability to use the vertical space was particularly important for this operation. The robots can move up, down and across, and the goods-to-person model reduces the amount of movement our people have to do. It gave us a solution that worked for the operation we were trying to build.
Humanoid technology is still maturing and not a fit for the problems we solve. As our use cases will continue to grow and change, we’ll continue to stay close to the evolution of this technology.
SC247: How do you decide whether automating a warehouse task is worth the cost?
Kapoor: Before I automate something, I want to understand why we are doing it that way in the first place. If there is waste in the process and you automate it, you are just automating the waste. Then you’ve put technology around it and made that waste harder to remove.
Once you understand and improve the process, you can establish your baseline and decide what technology needs to change. Then you can look at the investment and decide whether the technology is creating value.
Maple Grove is a good example. We established what we wanted to achieve before we implemented the automation and measured the results against that baseline. Productivity more than doubled, quality reached almost 100%, and speed was roughly three times what it had been. For me, that’s how you determine whether automation is worth the investment, if it’s actually solving the problem you started with and have results to prove it.
SC247: What advice would you give a warehouse operator considering robots for the first time?
Kapoor: Don’t start with the robot. Start with the problem and walk your process first. Understand where the waste is and take out what you can before you automate it. Then establish your baseline, because if you don’t know where you started, you won’t know what the technology has improved. You also have to look beyond the individual task. You could make one part of a warehouse significantly faster, but if the next part of the operation can’t handle the additional volume, you’ve just moved the bottleneck. The end goal is to create a better operation for your customer and your people. If automation helps you do that and the numbers make sense, then you have a strong case for it.
Manish Kapoor is Founder and CEO of Growth Catalyst Group .
